title: How Buffets Work
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the history and business of buffets, from the Scandinavian smorgasbord and its boost at the 1912 Stockholm Olympics and 1939 New York World's Fair Swedish pavilion, to Las Vegas all-you-can-eat buffets born from a late-1940s Last Frontier-era idea (credited to publicist Del Webb-era strip figure Herbert McDonald at the El Rancho), Depression-era all-you-can-eat deals, mid-century chains like Ponderosa, Bonanza, Sizzler and Golden Corral, salad and pizza buffets, fast-food buffets like Wendy's Superbar, and the economics of thin margins, adverse selection, and tricks restaurants use such as portion warnings, plate-clearing, carb-first lines, and drink markups. They also cover food safety issues like the danger zone temperature range, sneeze guards from Johnny Garn, food waste, and COVID-era pressure on buffets. The episode closes with a listener email from Kizzy about how an earlier episode on molecular gastronomy inspired her food technology career.

segments.title: Opening banter and buffet memories
segments.summary: Hosts riff on hitting the road again after the pandemic, then share personal memories of buffets, including family habits, a KFC buffet in Valdosta, Georgia, and a Bangladeshi lunch buffet.

segments.title: Smorgasbord origins and the 1912 Olympics and 1939 World's Fair
segments.summary: The smorgasbord's Scandinavian roots as brännvin boards for travelers, its aristocratic appeal, and how the spread to the 1912 Stockholm Olympics and the 1939 New York World's Fair Swedish pavilion's Three Crowns Restaurant popularized it in America.

segments.title: Las Vegas origins of the all-you-can-eat buffet
segments.summary: The Las Vegas buffet story: a publicist at the El Rancho who reportedly laid out cold cuts for gamblers in the late forties, the Midnight Chuck Wagon and the twenty-four-hour Buckaroo Buffet, and Vegas using cheap food to keep gamblers gambling.

segments.title: Depression-era all-you-can-eat deals and the rise of buffet chains
segments.summary: Early all-you-can-eat deals like Buffalo Wild Wings-style wing nights and a catfish night, the Depression-era oyster stew ad in Elyria, Ohio, and the 1950s and 1960s chain buffets with carb-heavy menus, with the name shifting from smorgasbord to buffet.
topics: all you can eat oyster stew

segments.title: Steakhouse, family and salad buffet chains
segments.summary: Steakhouse buffets such as Ponderosa and Bonanza, founded by Dan Blocker of Bonanza, along with Sizzler, Chuck-A-Rama, Golden Corral, Old Country Buffet, Hometown Buffet, Ryan's, and Western Sizzlin, plus Mexican and Mongolian buffets and Chi Chi's.

segments.title: Pizza buffets, salad buffets, and fast-food buffets
segments.summary: Pizza buffets such as Shakey's and Cici's, the rise and decline of salad buffets like Super Salad and Soup Plantation in the eighties and nineties, and fast-food buffet rumors plus Wendy's Superbar.

segments.title: Buffet economics, adverse selection and pricing tricks
segments.summary: Buffets have very thin profit margins; adverse selection theory predicts they should not exist. Restaurants use tactics such as Grandpa's two-dollar food waste charge, not clearing plates, carb-first lines, drink markups, and pricing that affects perceived food quality. Buffets also use fewer chefs and servers because food arrives pre-cooked.

segments.title: Banned customers, food safety and sneeze guards
segments.summary: Stories of customers banned from buffets, including Gobie in Brighton, Mr Wu's, Chuck-A-Rama and an Atkins couple, and a sushi buffet in Japan. Food safety concerns include shared tongs, the danger zone temperatures, and Johnny Garn's sneeze guard patent.

segments.title: Food waste, COVID-19 and the future of buffets
segments.summary: Ovation Brands' data modeling and food waste, gleaning laws, the CDC's COVID-era guidance against buffets, and the hosts' view that buffets may decline but persist on cruise ships and in casinos.

segments.title: Listener mail: Kizzy and molecular gastronomy
segments.summary: Listener Kizzy writes that a Stuff You Should Know episode on molecular gastronomy inspired her to pursue food science and technology, leading to an internship with a New Zealand food manufacturer.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listeners to email the show and close the episode.
